The Stylophone is a small analogue synthesizer, an electrophone. Put into production by Dubreq of London in 1968, it has a keyboard made from a printed circuit board, each note connected through a different resistor to a voltage-controlled oscillator; the player touches the keyboard with the tip of the pen, closing the circuit and producing the sound, and there are also a power switch, a tremolo control and a tuning potentiometer. It was marketed mainly as a toy at first, and was also used by musicians such as John Lennon, Kraftwerk and David Bowie; in Britain, Rolf Harris was its advertising face and appeared on a play-along record.

A beginner can start with the standard keyboard model, getting used to the tremolo control on the front and the tuning potentiometer on the back. With the bass, treble or later models, first check the sound, octave, volume or tempo setting; some models use touch pads, a slider or a built-in microphone for sampling instead, and the order is still to choose how it sounds, then touch the keyboard or the buttons.

電子筆琴為觸控筆演奏的類比合成器，1967年由布萊恩·賈維斯發明，1968年在倫: The Stylophone is an analogue synthesizer played with a stylus, invented by Brian Jarvis in 1967 and mass-produced in London from 1968, with about three million sold in its original run. It was marketed as a toy at first, and was also used by musicians such as John Lennon and David Bowie. A larger-keyboard version appeared in 1971, a piano attachment in 1972, a small amplifier in 1973, and production ended in 1975. In 2007 a toy company and the original maker relaunched it with a digitally recreated version made in China, and beatbox, theremin, cassette-shaped and modular models followed.
